title: Truly born, truly nailed
sum: After the greeting, Ignatius gives glory to 'Jesus Christ, the God who has made you so wise', and praises the Smyrnaeans for a faith 'nailed to the cross'. Then he sets out what they believe, almost like a creed: Christ is truly of David's family according to the flesh, Son of God by God's will and power, truly born of a virgin, baptized by John 'so that by him all righteousness might be fulfilled', and truly nailed for us under Pontius Pilate and Herod the tetrarch. The church is the fruit of that cross, gathered from Jews and nations into one body (1:2).
Every clause answers the teachers of chapter 2, who said it all only seemed to happen.

views.H: Lake's introduction names docetism among three motives that, all or some of them, he says can be traced in each letter; this letter answers it at the greatest length. Pilate and Herod fix the cross in public history.
views.N: Romans 1:3-4 (David's line and Son of God, in Lake's margin), Matthew 3:15 (the reason for the baptism, found only in Matthew), Luke 23:6-12 and Acts 4:27 (Herod and Pilate), Isaiah 5:26 (the flag, in the Greek), Ephesians 2:16 (one body).
views.C: See the topics The Incarnation and The Virgin Birth.

deep.b: Ignatius does not argue about natures or substances. He lists events and stamps each with 'truly': of David's family, born of a virgin, baptized, nailed under named rulers, raised. The list is close to Paul's summary of the good news in Romans 1:3-4 and to 1 Corinthians 15:3-4, and it adds the virgin birth and the baptism from the Gospels (Matthew 1:23; Matthew 3:15). Lightfoot, who compares To the Trallians 9 ('who was truly born') for the word 'born', notes that Ignatius 'doubtless had in his mind' Romans 1:3-4. For the teachers he opposes, God could not truly be born or truly die; for Ignatius the gospel is that he was and did.

echoes: Romans 1:3-4; Matthew 1:23; Matthew 3:13-17; Luke 3:1; Luke 23:6-12; Acts 4:27; 1 Timothy 6:13; Isaiah 5:26; Ephesians 2:14-16; 1 Corinthians 1:7

settings.what: Greeting and the confession of faith
settings.by: Ignatius, overseer of the church at Antioch, a prisoner under guard on his way to Rome
settings.to: The church at Smyrna, in Asia, where Ignatius had stayed on his journey
settings.when: From Troas (12:1), after Ignatius had stayed at Smyrna and met its church
settings.why: To confirm the Smyrnaeans in what they already believe ('You are fully convinced', 1:1) before he warns them of those who deny it. Praise comes first: he is arming friends, not correcting them.
settings.readers: The church at Smyrna and its overseer, unnamed here (12:2), whom Ignatius's letter To Polycarp and Eusebius name as Polycarp (Church History 3.36.10)

title: Only in appearance
sum: 'He suffered all these things for our sake, so that we might be saved. And he truly suffered, just as he also truly raised himself.' Some unbelievers say 'that he suffered only in appearance'; Ignatius answers that 'They themselves are only in appearance!', and that their end will match their belief: 'they will be bodiless, like demons' (2:1).
This one verse names, and answers, the teaching later called docetism, from the Greek word used here, dokein, 'to seem'.

views.H: Ignatius does not name the teachers (5:3). The Catholic Encyclopedia's article on the Docetae dates the name 'Docetae' to Serapion of Antioch (190-203) and later writers; here it is still a description, not a party name.
views.N: 1 John 4:2-3 and 2 John 7 test teachers by whether they confess 'Jesus Christ as having come in the flesh'.
views.C: See the topic Docetism and the topic The Incarnation.

settings.what: Against those who say he suffered in appearance
settings.by: Ignatius, overseer of the church at Antioch, a prisoner under guard on his way to Rome
settings.to: The church at Smyrna, in Asia, where Ignatius had stayed on his journey
settings.why: To name the error the confession answers, and to turn the word 'seeming' back on those who use it.

title: Take hold, feel me and see
sum: Ignatius knows and believes that Christ was in the flesh even after the resurrection (3:1). When he came to 'those with Peter', he said, 'Take hold, feel me and see that I am not a bodiless demon', and they touched him and believed; so they despised death (3:2). He ate and drank with them as a man of flesh, though in spirit united with the Father (3:3).

The saying is close to Luke 24:39 in sense but not in words, and its source was already a question for Eusebius, Origen and Jerome. The Berlin papyrus (B), copied in the 400s, covers 3:3 to 12:1 (Lake), so from here on a witness far older than the medieval copies can be compared; its readings are in the variants.

views.H: Eusebius quotes 3:1-2 and says the words come from he knows 'not whence' (Church History 3.36.11). Jerome assigns them to the Gospel he translated, the Gospel according to the Hebrews; Origen knew 'I am not a bodiless demon' from a 'Teaching of Peter' (both as Lightfoot quotes them).
views.N: Luke 24:36-43 and Acts 10:41 are in Lake's margin; John 20:27 has Thomas invited to touch.

deep.h: Where did the saying come from?
deep.b: Lightfoot sets out the evidence. Eusebius knew the Gospel according to the Hebrews, which was kept in the library at Caesarea, yet could not trace the saying. Origen ascribes 'I am not a bodiless demon' to a book called the Teaching of Peter, and says that book 'is not held among the church's books' (On First Principles, preface 8). Jerome twice ascribes it to the Gospel according to the Hebrews. Lightfoot suggests either that Jerome's memory failed him or that his copy of that Gospel had taken the saying in from Ignatius or from the Teaching of Peter. Of Ignatius himself he says, 'it is impossible to say whether he got it from oral tradition or from some written source', but its 'more elaborate language' shows it 'is later than the account in S. Luke'.

settings.what: The risen Christ in the flesh
settings.by: Ignatius, overseer of the church at Antioch, a prisoner under guard on his way to Rome
settings.to: The church at Smyrna, in Asia, where Ignatius had stayed on his journey
settings.why: To ground the church's faith in the witness of the first disciples, who touched the risen Christ and then 'looked down on death itself'.

title: Beasts in human form
sum: Ignatius warns the Smyrnaeans against 'beasts in human form': do not receive them or even meet them, but pray for them, 'in case they may somehow repent' (4:1). Then the argument from his chains: 'if these things were done by our Lord only in appearance, then I too am in chains only in appearance.' Why give himself to fire, sword and beasts? 'Because near the sword is near God, and in the midst of wild beasts is in the midst of God.' He endures it all in Christ's name, and 'the perfect human being' makes him strong (4:2).

views.H: Lake's footnotes show the Berlin papyrus at work: with the long recension it reads the dative 'in appearance' where Lake keeps G's accusative, and Lake's footnote names only G and L for 'who became' before 'the perfect human being' (4:2; see the variants).
views.N: Philippians 4:13 (Lake's margin) for 'makes me strong'; 1 Corinthians 15:30-32 for the same argument from danger.
views.C: Shunning false teachers while praying for them: compare 2 John 10-11 and 1 Timothy 2:1-4.

echoes: Philippians 4:13; 1 Corinthians 15:30-32; 2 John 10-11; Acts 20:29; Ignatius to the Romans 4:1-2

settings.by: Ignatius, overseer of the church at Antioch, a prisoner under guard on his way to Rome
settings.to: The church at Smyrna, in Asia, where Ignatius had stayed on his journey
settings.why: To protect the church from the teachers and to show that his own coming death makes sense only if Christ truly suffered.

title: Flesh-bearing
sum: Some deny Christ without knowing him; rather, he has denied them. Neither the prophets, the law of Moses, the gospel, nor the martyrs' sufferings have persuaded them (5:1). Praise of Ignatius is worth nothing from one who blasphemes his Lord by not confessing that he was 'flesh-bearing'; such a person 'is himself a carrier of a corpse' (5:2). Ignatius will not write their names, or even remember them, until they repent and turn back to 'the suffering, which is our resurrection' (5:3).

views.H: The teachers apparently respected Ignatius ('if he praises me', 5:2). Lake says it is disputed whether they were the same people as the Judaizers of his other letters.
views.N: 1 John 4:2 ('come in the flesh'), Matthew 10:33 (denying and being denied).

settings.by: Ignatius, overseer of the church at Antioch, a prisoner under guard on his way to Rome
settings.to: The church at Smyrna, in Asia, where Ignatius had stayed on his journey
settings.why: To make clear that no admiration for Ignatius can make up for denying Christ's flesh.

title: Faith and love are the whole thing
sum: Even heavenly powers face judgment if they do not believe in the blood of Christ; 'Let the one who makes room for this make room for it.' No rank should make anyone proud: 'The whole thing is faith and love' (6:1). Then a test the teachers fail: they hold other opinions about the grace of Christ, and 'They do not care about love: not for the widow, not for the orphan, not for the oppressed, not for the one in chains or the one set free, not for the hungry or the thirsty' (6:2).

views.N: Matthew 19:12 (Lake's margin), Colossians 1:16 (seen and unseen rulers), James 1:27 and Matthew 25:35-36 (the neglected people).
views.C: Ignatius joins right belief to care for the poor: the church's widows and prisoners were its daily work (13:1; Polycarp to the Philippians 4:3).

echoes: Colossians 1:16; 1 Corinthians 6:3; Matthew 19:12; James 1:27; Matthew 25:35-36; 1 John 3:17-18

settings.by: Ignatius, overseer of the church at Antioch, a prisoner under guard on his way to Rome
settings.to: The church at Smyrna, in Asia, where Ignatius had stayed on his journey
settings.why: To give the church a practical test of the teachers: how they treat the poor.

title: The flesh of our Savior
sum: The teachers 'keep away from the thanksgiving and from prayer, because they do not confess that the thanksgiving is the flesh of our Savior Jesus Christ, which suffered for our sins and which the Father raised in his kindness'. Arguing against God's gift, they die; it would be better for them to love, so that they might rise (7:1). Keep away from them, listen to the prophets and above all to the gospel, and run from divisions (7:2).
The churches read 7:1 in different ways: see the readings below and the views note at 7:1.
readings: Read as a statement about the bread

The thanksgiving 'is the flesh' of Christ: the bread and cup are his body and blood. On this reading Ignatius is an early witness to the real presence (Pohle in the Catholic Encyclopedia; the Missouri Synod's commemoration).
Read as an argument about the incarnation

The point is the reality of Christ's flesh: a meal that proclaims his body has no meaning for those who deny he had one. Lightfoot: 'The eucharist implies the reality of Christ's flesh. To those who deny this reality, it has no meaning at all.'

views.H: Lightfoot infers from 8:1 that the teachers held 'a eucharist of their own apart from the Church', and that 'abstain' means they kept away from the church's.
views.N: Matthew 26:26-28, John 6:51-58 and 1 Corinthians 10:16-17 and 11:23-29 lie behind 'the flesh of our Savior'.
views.C: See the views note at 7:1 for the readings of the churches, and the card at Matthew 26:26 on Christ's presence in the Supper. No new card is given here, because that question is already asked there.

settings.what: They keep away from the thanksgiving
settings.by: Ignatius, overseer of the church at Antioch, a prisoner under guard on his way to Rome
settings.to: The church at Smyrna, in Asia, where Ignatius had stayed on his journey
settings.why: To show the church that the teachers' absence from its meal follows from their belief, and to keep the church from following them into a separate gathering.

title: Where the overseer is
sum: 'All of you, follow the overseer the way Jesus Christ follows the Father. Follow the council of elders as if it were the apostles. Respect the deacons as God's command.' Nothing that belongs to the church is to be done without the overseer: 'Count that thanksgiving valid which is under the overseer, or under someone he entrusts it to' (8:1). 'Wherever the overseer appears, there let the people be, just as wherever Jesus Christ is, there is the catholic church.' No baptism and no love feast without him (8:2). It is good to know God and the overseer; to act behind his back is to serve the devil (9:1). Ignatius thanks them for their care (9:2).

These lines hold the one overseer with elders and deacons, the 'valid' thanksgiving, and 'the catholic church', which the Catholic Encyclopedia and the Missouri Synod call the first use of the phrase.
readings: Read as church order for all times

Ignatius states how the church must be ordered: the thanksgiving and baptism belong under the bishop or one he appoints. The Catechism quotes these lines (Catechism 1369); Orthodox practice keeps the same rule through the bishop's antimension (Orthodox Church in America, 'Holy Orders').

Ignatius writes to a church where some held their own meal apart (Lightfoot on 8:1). His rule ties the church's worship to its overseer, so that the separate meal is seen for what it is. Read this way the stress falls on unity in one city's church; how far the rule binds churches ordered in other ways is the question of the card below.

views.H: The three offices appear here as Ignatius knows them in Asia: one overseer, a council of elders, deacons. When the one overseer emerged in each city is a debated question (see the cards at Acts 20:28 and Philippians 1:1).
views.N: In the New Testament 'overseers' and 'elders' seem to be the same leaders (Acts 20:17, 28; Titus 1:5-7). 'Love feasts' are in Jude 1:12; the Supper as part of a meal in 1 Corinthians 11:17-34.
views.C: See the card below on who may lead the Supper and baptize; the views notes at 8:1 and 8:2; and the cards on bishops and elders at 1 Timothy 3, Acts 20, Philippians 1 and Titus 1.

deep.b: The phrase hē katholikē ekklēsia appears here, as far as the Catholic Encyclopedia and the Missouri Synod's commemoration say, for the first time. Lightfoot: here it is 'the general or universal Church, as opposed to a particular body of Christians'; the later technical sense, 'as opposed to the heretical sects', came after. The sentence is a comparison: the local people gather round their overseer as the whole church gathers round Jesus Christ. The Plain English Translation writes it lowercase, as in the Martyrdom of Polycarp, so that the word is not read as the name of one communion. The Catechism quotes the line for its teaching that the Church is catholic 'because Christ is present in her' (Catechism 830).

deep.h: The love feast and the thanksgiving
deep.b: 'It is not lawful to baptize or to hold a love feast without the overseer.' Lake's footnote says the love feast 'was given to some kind of religious meal' and that 'The context here suggests that it is a synonym for the Eucharist, but the point is doubted by some scholars.' Lightfoot holds that in Ignatius's day the thanksgiving was still part of the shared meal, as in Corinth (1 Corinthians 11:17-34), so that baptism and the love feast are 'the two most important functions in which the bishop could bear a part'.

traditions.q: Ignatius counts as 'valid' only the thanksgiving 'under the overseer, or under someone he entrusts it to', and says no one may baptize or hold a love feast without the overseer (8:1-2). Who may lead the Lord's Supper and baptize today? (On the office of bishop see the cards at Acts 20:28, Philippians 1:1 and 1 Timothy 3; on ordination, 1 Timothy 4:14; on who may receive, 1 Corinthians 11:27-29.)
views: Only a validly ordained priest or bishop presides: 'Only validly ordained priests can preside at the Eucharist' (Catechism 1411). 'The bishop of the place is always responsible for the Eucharist, even when a priest presides', and the Catechism quotes this very sentence of Ignatius (Catechism 1369). For baptism 'the ordinary ministers' are 'the bishop and priest and, in the Latin Church, also the deacon' (Catechism 1256).

The bishop is the leader; the priests 'assist the bishop', 'preside at the celebration of the liturgy', and are 'assigned by the bishop'. On each altar lies the antimension 'signed by the bishop which is the permission to the community to gather and to act as the Church of God. Without the antimension, the priest and his people cannot function legitimately' (Orthodox Church in America, The Orthodox Faith, 'Holy Orders').

Only one episcopally ordained is a lawful minister: 'No man shall be accounted or taken to be a lawful Bishop, Priest, or Deacon in the Church of England, or suffered to execute any of the said functions, except he be called, tried, examined, and admitted thereunto, according to the Form hereafter following, or hath had formerly Episcopal Consecration or Ordination' (Preface to the Ordinal, Book of Common Prayer, 1662). At ordination the bishop gives the priest 'authority to preach the Word of God, and to minister the holy Sacraments in the Congregation, where thou shalt be lawfully appointed thereunto'; the deacon is to 'assist the Priest ... when he ministereth the holy Communion' and 'in the absence of the Priest to baptize infants' (the same Ordinal). Article XXIII adds that no one may minister the Sacraments 'before he be lawfully called, and sent to execute the same'.
'No one should publicly teach in the Church or administer the Sacraments unless he be regularly called' (Augsburg Confession, Article XIV).
There are two sacraments, baptism and the Lord's Supper, 'neither of which may be dispensed by any, but by a minister of the Word lawfully ordained' (Westminster Confession 27.4).
Baptism and the Lord's Supper 'are to be administered by those only who are qualified and thereunto called, according to the commission of Christ' (Second London Baptist Confession, 28.2).

echoes: Philippians 1:1; Acts 20:17; Acts 20:28; Titus 1:5-7; 1 Timothy 3:1-13; Jude 1:12; 1 Corinthians 11:17-34; Matthew 18:20

settings.by: Ignatius, overseer of the church at Antioch, a prisoner under guard on his way to Rome
settings.to: The church at Smyrna, in Asia, where Ignatius had stayed on his journey
settings.when: After the warning against those who keep away from the church's thanksgiving
settings.why: To keep the Smyrnaeans together around their own overseer, council and deacons, so that no separate meal or baptism could pass as the church's. Knowing that a rival gathering existed (7:1; Lightfoot on 8:1) changes how the rule reads: it guards a church under pressure.
settings.readers: The Smyrnaean church: its overseer, council of elders and deacons (12:2), and its members, some of whom may have been drawn to the separate gatherings

title: Come back to your senses
sum: It makes sense to come back to our senses while there is time to repent. 'It is good to know God and the overseer.' Whoever honors the overseer is honored by God; whoever acts behind his back serves the devil (9:1). Ignatius thanks the Smyrnaeans for refreshing him: 'God is your reward' (9:2).

views.H: In 9:2 Lake follows the papyrus, 'God is your reward', against later witnesses with a verb (see the variant).

settings.by: Ignatius, overseer of the church at Antioch, a prisoner under guard on his way to Rome
settings.to: The church at Smyrna, in Asia, where Ignatius had stayed on his journey
settings.why: To press the call to unity, and to thank the church for its care while he was with them.

title: Philo and Rheus Agathopus
sum: The Smyrnaeans did well to welcome Philo and Rheus Agathopus, who followed Ignatius for the word of God, as deacons of God; they give thanks for them (10:1). Ignatius offers his spirit and chains as 'a life in exchange' for the church, which was not ashamed of his chains; nor will Christ, 'the perfect hope', be ashamed of them (10:2).

views.H: Ignatius's letter To the Philadelphians (chapter 11) calls Philo 'the deacon from Cilicia' and Rheus Agathopus 'an elect man who is following me from Syria' (Lake). The papyrus reads 'Gaius' for 'Rheus' (see the variant).
views.N: 2 Timothy 1:16 (Lake's margin): Onesiphorus was not ashamed of Paul's chain.

settings.by: Ignatius, overseer of the church at Antioch, a prisoner under guard on his way to Rome
settings.to: The church at Smyrna, in Asia, where Ignatius had stayed on his journey
settings.when: Philo and Rheus had come on after Ignatius
settings.why: To thank the church for welcoming his companions and to bind himself to them in love.

title: Send an envoy of God
sum: Their prayer has reached the church at Antioch. Ignatius, the last of that church and worthy only by God's grace, asks for grace to reach God (11:1). News has come that Antioch is at peace: let the Smyrnaeans elect 'an envoy of God' to go to Syria and rejoice with them that their 'body' is restored (11:2), and send him with a letter. 'You are mature, so think mature thoughts as well' (11:3).

views.H: The letter does not say what Antioch's trouble had been. The Orthodox Church in America's life says that at Troas Ignatius 'heard the happy news of the end of the persecution'. The same request goes to Polycarp in To Polycarp 7 (Lightfoot) and to the Philadelphians.
views.N: Philippians 3:15 (Lake's margin); 2 Corinthians 8:19 for a messenger chosen by the churches.
views.C: The church 'elects' (cheirotonēsai) its own envoy: compare Acts 14:23 and the card there on who chooses ministers.

settings.by: Ignatius, overseer of the church at Antioch, a prisoner under guard on his way to Rome
settings.to: The church at Smyrna, in Asia, where Ignatius had stayed on his journey
settings.when: At Troas, after news of peace at Antioch
settings.why: To draw the Smyrnaean church into the care of his own church far away, now that he can no longer lead it.

title: Greetings from Troas
sum: The brothers at Troas send greetings; Ignatius writes 'by Burrhus', sent with him by the Smyrnaeans and the Ephesians, a 'model of service to God' (12:1). He greets the overseer, the council of elders, the deacons, his 'fellow slaves', and all, in Christ's flesh and blood, suffering and resurrection (12:2).

views.H: Eusebius says Ignatius wrote from Troas to the Philadelphians, to Smyrna and to Polycarp (Church History 3.36.10). The overseer greeted in 12:2 is not named.
views.C: The order of greeting, overseer, elders, deacons, people, matches 8:1.

settings.by: Ignatius, overseer of the church at Antioch, a prisoner under guard on his way to Rome
settings.to: The church at Smyrna, in Asia, where Ignatius had stayed on his journey
settings.when: At Troas, as Burrhus prepares to carry the letter
settings.why: To bind the church's members, leaders and households to him, and through him to one another.
settings.readers: The named households and the women of 13:1-2: the 'virgins who are called widows', the household of Tavia, and Alce, who is greeted again in To Polycarp 8 (Lightfoot)

title: The virgins who are called widows
sum: Ignatius greets the families of the brothers, with wives and children, and 'the virgins who are called widows', and says farewell 'in the power of the Father'; Philo greets them (13:1). He greets the household of Tavia, praying that she be firm in faith and love, and Alce, 'a name dear to me', Daphnus 'who has no equal', and Eutecnus (13:2).

views.H: Alce may be the Alce of the Martyrdom of Polycarp 17:2, sister of Nicetes and aunt of the officer Herod (Lightfoot). 'Tavia' may be 'Gavia' (see the variant).
views.C: The 'widows' were an enrolled group in the church (1 Timothy 5:3-16); on the puzzling phrase see the views note at 13:1.

echoes: 1 Timothy 5:3-16; Acts 9:39-41; Colossians 4:15; Martyrdom of Polycarp 17:2
